learningObjective: Determine when a reshape/transpose can be a pure view over the same physical storage and when materialization (a copy) is required.

canonicalClaims.claim: A tensor operation is a pure view iff the requested (shape, stride) pair addresses the same physical buffer as the source without re-ordering elements; otherwise the operation requires materialization (a copy).
conditions: The source tensor's storage layout is known and stable.
The framework's view semantics require a single (shape, stride) pair per view.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a view is always faster to consume; downstream ops may prefer materialized (contiguous) tensors for cache/coalescing.
Does not imply that PyTorch's `.reshape` never copies; it copies precisely when a view is not expressible.

misconceptions.claim: PyTorch `.reshape` on a contiguous tensor never copies.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Reshapes that require a new element ordering (like reshape(4,6) on contiguous [2,3,4]) copy.
Transpose is expressible as a permutation of the stride tuple over the same storage — the canonical example of a view.

misconceptions.claim: Any change to shape metadata forces materialization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Many shape changes are pure metadata operations when compatible with the underlying strides.

misconceptions.claim: Views and materializations are interchangeable from a downstream kernel's perspective.
misconceptions.whyWrong: A non-contiguous view can hurt vectorization / coalescing; materialization may improve downstream throughput at the cost of copy bandwidth.

implementationFacts: PyTorch `.view` requires contiguity; `.reshape` returns a view when possible, copy otherwise
Transpose is a metadata-only operation on strides
MLIR memref supports strided layouts with an offset + strides
performanceScenarios: Determining view vs. copy is a routine question for compiler-level buffer planning and for user-level performance tuning.
